rows.title: Leadership and Integrity
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: discuss the ethical, legal, social, and moral complexity of processes within the Administration of Justice system and how they relate to other fields;
explain the impact of effective interpersonal communication within the Administration of Justice system;
recognize the behaviors and decisions that impact personal success and organizational integrity;
describe the potential impact on community trust when personal and organizational integrity is violated;
describe behaviors that improve communication and interactions within the community;
explain five elements of organizational culture that impact the effectiveness of individuals and teams;
describe the difference between management and leadership;
demonstrate the impact of transactional leadership and transformational leadership on individuals and organizations;
identify ethical issues that often arise in regard to professional responsibility, public service, or law;
state basic general ethical principles and to apply these to particular cases;
demonstrate mastery of at least one method for resolving ethical disagreements;
explain the importance - both for one's self and for society as a whole - of being ethical;
propose and defend standards for justice.

rows.title: Investigative Reporting
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: record and use investigation notes;
recite the advantages and disadvantages of form and narrative types of reporting;
describe the physical content of arrest, incident, and other reports and the rationale for different reporting styles;
explain the requirements for effective communication and how to find and assemble information;
record information accurately and legibly enough in a police report to present to others in the legal community for purpose of follow-up investigation and the issuance of complaints;
demonstrate how to provide effective testimony in court as a witness;
demonstrate the ability to write clear, concise and detailed investigative reports with a high level of grammatical accuracy.

rows.title: Evidence
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: describe various kinds of evidence;
define and explain direct and circumstantial evidence;
explain the concept of relevancy with regard to evidence;
explain the rules covering the admissibility of evidence in court;
explain the qualifications related to witness competency;
explain the concept of "chain of custody" and its relationship to the admissibility of evidence;
explain the exclusionary rule as it relates to search and seizure, identification procedures and the admissibility of evidence;
demonstrate an understanding how to testify effectively.

rows.title: Gangs and Drugs
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: discuss the historical background and identification of various kinds of gangs;
explain the central issues and strategies in gang prevention and enforcement;
discuss the major components of gangs, including recruitment organization, hierarchy, symbols and rituals, and relationships with other gangs;
list the most important local, national and international gangs;
explain the relationship of gang activity to drug trafficking;
develop strategies for crime prevention in gang-related areas.

rows.title: Family Violence
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Understand the family as a system and describe the relationship between patterns of family interaction and violence;

demonstrate an understanding of the historical view of the legal status of children and other conditions leading to family violence, including child abuse, with emphasis on coping with such situations;
Describe the existing resources in the community to control family violence and child abuse and the means for effective intervention in the field.
Develop skills associated with specific types of intervention (for example, mandated reporting);
Learn how to recognize, refer, and/or report violent situations to professionals with specific skills in providing long term services.

rows.title: Biological/Physical Anthropology
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: explain and apply the methodology of physical anthropology inquiry;
explain the theory of evolution, including sources and types of evidence, major evolutionary trends and the mechanics of evolution;
identify and critically evaluate biological and social issues relating to human evolution;
evaluate human anatomy and behavior in the context of primate anatomy and behavior;
evaluate hominin/hominid adaptations and evolutionary trends.

rows.title: Forensic Anthropology Laboratory
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Use anatomy to identify human remains;
follow recovery, ethical, and legal procedures as established in standard archeological methodology, and the forensic protocol;
identify minimum and maximum number of individuals in a sample;
identify age at death and sex, and estimate stature and ancestry, following forensic guidelines;
analyze different types of pathologies and identify their causes, following forensic guidelines;
measure time since death, and identify cause and manner of death, using forensic guidelines.

rows.title: Social and Cultural Anthropology
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Define the scope of anthropology and discuss the role of cultural anthropology within the discipline;
Recognize the methods, theories and perspectives used to study and understand human cultures;
Employ the relativist perspective while discussing cultural variation;
Explain the importance of the ethnographic method in the study of culture;
Demonstrate an understanding of anthropological concepts including ethnicity, gender, political organization, economic systems, kinship, rituals and belief systems;
Explain the interconnectedness of the economic, political and sociocultural forces of globalization amongst diverse cultural groups;
Analyze and evaluate the ethical issues anthropologists encounter, and professional ethical obligations that must be met in the study of and application in cultural groups different from their own.

rows.title: Bus Maintenance
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: apply basic principles of measuring, tooling, hardware, materials, and system components toward maintaining heavy-duty diesel engines;
Implement the appropriate standard operating procedures for preventive maintenance Inspections to include California Highway Patrol out-of-service criteria;
identify, inspect, and maintain coach components;
access and use fleet service manuals;
process major inspection forms.

rows.title: Bus Basic Electrical
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: understand the fundamental principles and applications of electricity;
apply Ohms, Kirchhoff, and Watts laws;
demonstrate the function and operation of essential electrical components;
demonstrate the proper use and functions of digital multimeters, carbon piles load testers;
perform battery testing using a Midtronics battery impedance tester;
test battery electrolyte strength using a hydrometer;
understand the operation and use of electric and electronic components, and use them to build simple circuits;
understand the use of connectors, switching devices, and electric controls;
understand the basic operation of wiring schematics;
understand the basic operation of electrical systems typical of heavy-duty coach buses;
understand the basic operation of starting system operation and their troubleshooting;
understand the basic operation of charging systems and their troubleshooting;
understand the use and selection of circuit protection devices.

rows.title: Bus Transmissions
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: understand the fundamentals of heavu-duty automatic transmission and their component operation and diagnosis;
identify and understand the function of a transmission's internal components;
understand the importance of proper transmission preventive maintenance;
develop a basic knowledge of hydraulic fluid flow;
demonstrate how transmission electrical control circuits work and are diagnosed;
explain the use of laptop-based transmission troubleshooting software;
perform diagnostic test procedures to identify specific transmission failure.

rows.title: Automotive Air and Fuel Delivery Systems
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: inspect engine assembly for fuel, oil, coolant, and other leaks;
diagnose abnormal exhaust color, odor, and sound;
inspect and test mechanical and electrical fuel pumps and pump control systems for pressure, regulation and volume, and perform necessary action;
replace fuel filters;
check and adjust idle speed and fuel;
inspect the integrity of the exhaust manifold, exhaust pipes, muffler(s), catalytic converter(s), resonator(s), tail pipe(s), and heat shield(s); perform necessary action;
inspect throttle body, air induction system, intake manifold and gaskets for vacuum leaks and/or unmetered air;
describe fuel injection operation;
diagnose throttle body fuel injection systems;
diagnosis port fuel injection systems.

rows.title: Hybrid and Electric Vehicles
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: contrast how a hybrid or electric vehicle operates when compared to conventional vehicles;
demonstrate proper safety procedures and use of PPE when working on and around high voltage vehicles;
identify, discuss, and measure how high voltage systems operate;
compare and contrast AC and DC electrical systems;
explain in detail how hybrid electric drive systems operate, including electric motors, generators and controls;
critically analyze how regenerative braking systems work;
contrast and identify how hybrid transmission and transaxles operate;
perform preventive, normal, and specific hybrid and electric vehicle service and maintenance;
assess and examine scan tool data, retrieve and record stored diagnostic trouble codes for hybrid and electric vehicle systems;
access and use service information to perform step-by-step diagnosis.
compare and contrast the different types of high voltage batteries used in hybrid and electric vehicles;
perform the removal of, and the appropriate tests of, the high voltage system components;
perform a cooling system service for the high voltage system;
evaluate the condition of motor windings;
compare and contrast the pros and cons of gasoline and diesel engines.

rows.title: Electrician Apprenticeship III
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: understand A/C circuits;
analyze all facets of an A/C circuit;
understand NFPA 70E guidelines;
understand how to implement NFPA 70E on a job site;
understand the basics of transformers;
demonstrate proper installation of transformers in compliance with the NEC articles.

rows.title: Electrician Apprenticeship VI
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: describe basic over-current protection;
describe grounding requirements of the NEC;
describe the bonding requirements of NEC;
describe the grounding rules for medium and high voltage systems;
demonstrate how to correctly calculate conductor ampacities;
demonstrate how to correctly calculate overcurrent protection;
demonstrate how to correctly calculate equipment grounding conductors;
demonstrate how to correctly calculate Conduit Fill;
describe and apply addiitional articles of the NEC.

rows.title: Electrician Apprenticeship IX
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: describe the basic principles building automation;
describe how to integrate lighting systems, HVAC system components, and security systems;
demonstrate the ability to program all types of components within the system;
describe the torque concepts and application;
demonstrate proper hoisting techniques utilizing a crane;
demonstrate the appropriate hand signals while hoisting and lifting;
describe and apply additional articles of the 2014 NEC related to building automation systems.

rows.title: Electrical Materials, Blueprint Reading, Cabling Systems
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: identify wire types and cable used in fire alarm & life safety systems;
identify and explain the use of various fasteners and anchors;
interpret blueprints for industry systems;
identify methods of hand bending conduit and use math formulas to determine conduit bends and offsets;
identify the specific use of various knots and slings in simple rigging;
identify and describe the safe handling of low voltage cabling and related low voltage codes.

rows.title: Networking Principles, Fiber Optic Implementation, and Video Applications
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: calculate the voltage drop in a cable for various applications;
interpret and apply NEC code governing conductors and cables;
explain the operation principles and function of network topologies;
describe the design, operation and performance of a fiber optic transmitter and receiver;
explain the testing procedures for fiber-optic systems;
describe video systems grounding problems and solutions for interference suppression;
explain the basic operating principles and applications of wireless communication systems;
identify the equipment used when troubleshooting wireless systems;
identify the basic components of a security system.

rows.title: Medical Terminology & the Human Body
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: describe the components of medical terms;
build medical terms using word parts;
define a medical term by dividing it into its elements;
spell and pronounce medical terms;
apply medical terms and abbreviations appropriately;
identify word roots, suffixes, prefixes, anatomical, diagnostic, medical, surgical, and additional terms as they relate to each body system;
identify systems, structures and organs of the human body;
discuss function of the systems of the human body.

rows.title: Introduction to Psychology-Counseling in a Multicultural Environment
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: apply Psychology-Counseling theory and techniques;
describe fundamental Psychology-Counseling techniques and theories;
describe methods of effective behavioral change;
identify the demographic composition of one’s campus and environment;
develop a fundamental plan of action with an individual to affect that individual’s behavioral change or desired life change;
assess socio-economic/cultural barriers;
identify local intervention or social service programs;
express the importance of an individualized action plan for behavioral change.

rows.title: Health Coach Training I
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: understand the concept and importance of Health Coaches;
identify personal, social, and environmental barriers to health faced by patients in Alameda County;
apply foundational health coach skills to interactions with non-insulin dependent diabetes patients;
demonstrate an understanding of the anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology, causes and treatment protocols for non-insulin dependent diabetes.

rows.title: Health Coach Training IV
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate an understanding of the anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology, causes and treatment protocols for hypertension;
apply advanced health coach skills to interactions with hypertension patients;
independently conduct home visits to check patient wellbeing, action plan compliance, and patient needs, health changes and improvements;
independently conduct follow-up with the patient regarding referrals, appointments, and services received;
develop long-term career and educational goals;
confidently conduct a health education seminar.

rows.title: Machine Tool Technology II
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: properly use precision measuring tools, such as the Bore Micrometers, Large Vernier calipers, dial height gauge, .0001” dial test indicator, and various types of micrometers, also optical / video measuring machines;
perform advanced bench operations, such as draw filing, contour sawing and geometric die head threading;
set up and perform advanced drill press, lathe and vertical milling machine operations;
machine to a precision layout on the surface grinders using precision tools, such as the vernier protractor, parallels, and Angle and Gage Blocks;
apply intermediate mathematical formulas for calculating correct pitch, leads, and gear-cutting data required for precision part manufacture;
evaluate a blueprint to make a manufacturing plan to produce the desired machine part;
safely setup and operate a Hardinge lathe to make a 60 Degree threaded shaft with no thread relief;
safely setup and operate a manual milling machine to make a prismatic part (like the 1-2-3 Block Set) manufactured within the part drawing tolerances and geometrically shaped part;
heat Treat the 1-2-3 Blocks and Precision Grind all external surfaces to within the
+/- .0002” Tolerance Zone per ANSI Y14.5M;

offhand grind a High Speed Steel Roughing and Threading Toolbit to a tolerance of +/- 1/2 degree for each of the tool’s six major cutting or clearance angles as described in the Machine Tool Laboratory Manual;
measure the Gears manufactured and evaluate whether the gear is acceptable to the print tolerances published, all geometries and published Gear Machining Standards like ANSI Y14.5M.

rows.title: Numerical Control Program I
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate the basic concepts of the Cartesian coordinate system;
compare cutter location coordinates using basic trig functions;
prepare basic three axis numerical control programs;
set up and run basic three axis computer numerical control drill and mill programs;
use computer software to prepare N/C machine control programs.

rows.title: Introduction to Welding
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: properly identify CC (constant current) and CV (constant voltage) welding power supllies and describe their applications;
handle welding and shop equipment in a safe manner;
identify common metals, metal alloys and their properties;
demonstrate proper usage of welding power supplies;
correctly identify and use electrodes, flux-core wires and welding consumables;
perform welds using welding symbols, blueprints and shop sketches;
identify hazardous material and apply OSHA safety norms in shop environment;
perform welds in flat and horizontal positions using SMAW, FCAW, GMAW, GMAW and OFW processes;
perform oxyacetylene and plasma cuts;
properly maintain shop and welding equipment.

rows.title: SolidWorks for Machine Shops
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: create solid models from engineering prints;
recognize and generate extrusions, revolves, sweeps, and lofts;
create engineering drawings with cross section, auxiliary, and detail views;
edit existing sketches and features;
create customized SolidWorks templates;
create assemblies and apply mates and fits;
generate assembly exploded views and movement simulations;

import dwg, iges, and dxf files;
create solid bodies from imported files;
create bolt holes, through holes, and threaded holes using the Hole Wizard;
Duplicate features using patterns and mirror images;
add hardware components using “Smart Fasteners” in assembly drawings;
create cosmetic simulated threads and an accurate size and shape thread on solid models;
run basic Cosmos Express finite element simulations;
print 3 dimensional ABS plastic fused deposited models (FDM) on a Dimension SST 1200;
create part and assembly eDrawings complete with dimensions and mark up comments.

rows.title: Introduction to Roofing/Waterproof Industry
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: describe the nature of the roofing and waterproofing industry;
identify the tools and items of equipment used in the trade;
name the various structural designs of roofs;
demonstrate safe work procedures and identify unsafe procedures and practices;
demonstrate proper operation and maintenance of kettles.

rows.title: Cold-Applied Roofing Systems
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Demonstrate the methods of roof preparation, the handling and the loading of cold-applied roof materials;
Describe the application procedures of cold-applied roof assemblies;
Identify tools and equipment commonly used in cold-applied roofing assemblies;
Identify safety rules that apply on cold-applied roofing assemblies.

rows.title: Maintenance/Repair/Re-Roofing
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Describe the procedures for the maintenance, repair and re-roofing of built-up, shingle, cold-applied, single-ply and rigid roofs, waterproofing and dampproofing;
Identify tools and equipment commonly used in roof maintenance and repair;
Identify safety rules that apply on roof maintenance and repair.

rows.title: Standard First Aid
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Identify emergency action principles, activate EMS, scene safety;
Demonstrate chest compressions, opening the airway and rescue breathing in adults;
Demonstrate techniques to clear airway obstructions in adults;
Demonstrate adult CPR, CPR barriers and AED techniques for adults;
Discuss and demonstrate assessment of a victim;
Demonstrate techniques to control bleeding and shock;

Identify care for a victim of burns, eye, mouth, head, neck, spine, and nose injuries, bites and stings, musculoskeletal injuries, poisoning, diabetic emergencies, allergic reactions, breathing emergencies, chest and abdominal wounds, strokes, seizures, and temperature extremes, and positioning or moving a victim;
Discuss ways to reduce risk of injury and major medical emergencies;
Describe methods to prevent exposure to blood borne pathogens;
Discuss the legal issues related to providing first aid and CPR;
Demonstrate glove removal, choking management, initial assessment of victim, how to stop bleeding and apply a bandage, how to use an auto-injector, effective PR, and use of an AED.

rows.title: Sprinkler Fitter Apprenticeship II
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: recognize the related safety and health aspects of the industry and demonstrate the necessary protective measures;
recognize and identify the different types of pipes, valves, and hangers used in the piping industry;
recognize and demonstrate the proper use and care of tools;
demonstrate accurate and efficient pipe threading while using fitting take-outs;
interpret NFPA 13D and NFPA 13R;
explain the history, installation, and hazard ratings of automatic fire sprinkler systems;
demonstrate CPVC installation to obtain certification;
analyze the work environment in order to employ proper safety measures.

rows.title: Sprinkler Fitter Apprenticeship V
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:

demonstrate the capabilities of an OSHA-defined Competent Person for underground fire protection work;
demonstrate proper setup and use of the oxygen-acetylene torch for cutting and welding of steel material;

demonstrate proper setup and use of the plasma torch for cutting steel material;

analyze the work environment in order to employ proper safety measures;
effectively use math to calculate 45 degree offsets around underground obstructions.

rows.title: Sprinkler Fitter Apprenticeship VIII
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

review horizontal splitcase, vertical turbine, vertical inline, and end suction fire pumps;
recognize the difference between electrical and diesel driven fire pumps;
recognize and demonstrate the safe operation of controllers and fire pumps;
interpret NFPA 20 rules and regulations governing the installation of stationary fire pumps and controllers;
review hydraulics for the sprinkler fitter;
analyze the work environment in order to employ proper safety measures.

rows.title: Residential Sprinkler Fitter Apprenticeship I
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

interpret standard fire sprinkler blueprints including symbols and abbreviations;
operate a ruler with accuracy of 1/16th of inch;
recognize the related safety and health aspects of the industry and demonstrate the necessary protective measures;
identify the standard and reducing fittings used in the fire protection industry;
recognize and demonstrate knowledge of basic pipe dimensions;
recognize automatic sprinkler systems and their components;
analyze the work environment in order to employ proper safety measures;
demonstrate CPVC (Chlorinated polyvinyl chloride) installation to obtain certification.

rows.title: Residential Sprinkler Fitter Apprenticeship IV
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

demonstrate proper preparation and joining of both soldered and brazed copper tube joints;
review automatic sprinkler systems;
review mathematics required for Sprinkler Fitter;
recognize design concepts and operational characteristics of wet pipe alarm valves;
analyze the work environment in order to employ proper safety measures;
safely operate a telehandler.

rows.title: Fiber Installation & Maintenance
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

identify the major components of a Fiber Optic System;
describe how generic Fiber Optic Systems operate;
perform installation tests and troubleshooting of the following:
Fiber cable and optical interface equipment,
Optical terminating and monitoring equipment,
Multiplexers and associated protection systems;

Optical loss test set,
Error rate test set,
Fault locate test set;

test fiber optic cable using an OTDR;
install and maintain security systems including intrusion detection, access control and video surveillance Systems;
describe security design fundamentals;
discuss the principles of operation of intrusion detection systems, infrastructure and devices;

rows.title: Fiber Installation & Maintenance - Level 2

Describe the types and characteristics of fiber optic cables.

draw proportional freehand and constructed images;

rows.title: Advanced Oil  Painting I

outcomes: use terminology, tools, techniques, supports and grounds for oil painting with competence;
apply a variety of tools and techniques to alter a painting’s two-dimensional surface to an illusionistic space;
define and pursue individual project goals and successfully design and execute a final project start to finish;
complete paintings in a variety of subject matter including, still life, landscape, figural and non-representational art;
create a series of work based upon their own concepts and ideas;

rows.title: Acrylic Painting - Beginning II
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

identify and solve intermediate pictorial problems related to traditional and contemporary representational painting methods, materials, and concepts;
experiment with and construct paintings utilizing non-traditional pictorial formats and concepts including; abstract, non-objective, multiple-panel or mixed media paintings;
produce paintings based on individual interpretation of topical assignments and problems;
develop and express conceptual and material intentions in written and oral formats and apply these to the creation of a finished series of paintings;
evaluate paintings orally and in writing using correct terminology related to concepts, materials and techniques;
critique finished paintings and receive criticism from others;
understand and apply all safety rules and precautions related to the handling, storage and disposal of all painting materials and residues.

rows.title: Introduction to Ceramics I
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: differentiate clay varieties and ceramic processes;
create ceramic forms utilizing pinch, coil, soft slab, hard slab and throwing techniques;
analyze and demonstrate existing ceramic pieces and distinguish the forming processes used in creating them throughout history;
produce and apply surface treatment to a variety of different forms;
examine and describe historical and contemporary developments, trends, materials, and approaches in ceramics;
assess and critique ceramics in group, individual, and written contexts using relevant critique formats, concepts and terminology;
safely handle and use all studio equipment, tools, and materials.

rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

demonstrate an advanced execution of decoration techniques appropriate for specific forms for the advanced level of study;
apply critical thinking skills to the critique and evaluation of their artwork and the artwork of others;
apply advanced design decisions in the construction of a line of functional pottery forms;
create an original line of production pottery forms with a signature style;
examine contemporary approaches to production pottery and forms from diverse cultures.

rows.title: Wood and Stone Sculpture I
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: achieve basic technical skills of carving with hand tools, power tools and sharpening and maintenance skills and the basic terms and technology of carving wood and stone;
use wood and stone to create personal authentic expressions through a variety of themes, both figurative and abstract;
compare and contrast the multicultural influence of Eastern and Western sculpture traditions on contemporary art;
analyze masterpieces and students’ sculptures, and recognize the elements and principles of three-dimensional designs.

rows.title: Metal Sculpture - Lost Wax Bronze Casting
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:

make a rubber mold from that original;
employ the fundamental techniques of lost wax casting;
recognize and identify the attributes of fine craftsmanship;
critique their own work and the work of others;
apply concepts of contemporary sculpture to class projects;
demonstrate individual creative application of personal style (how the students made the assignment their own).

rows.title: Color Theory

apply individual aesthetic decisions and judgments related to their own artwork;
use skillfully a variety of artistic materials, techniques and tools;
produce finished color assignments that demonstrate an understanding of color theory and principles in the history of art;
comprehend and describe how color is perceived culturally, and symbolically;
understand color usage in contemporary art and design.

refine existing skills and techniques;
define and pursue individual project goals and successfully design and execute a final project start to finish;
utilize museums and galleries as a learning source.

use color with skill in figurative compositions and in singular figurative drawings;
use skills to express emotions in composition and figure;
apply the skills of drawing the figure and figure compositions to professional and collegiate goals.
Build an individual portfolio of figurative drawings.

rows.title: Illustration
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: develop a conceptual idea for an assigned project, verbalize it and visually communicate it on paper;
take a sketched idea and develop it through thumbnails, a layout, a comprehensive, to finished art;
work successfully with a variety of illustration mediums;
list different kinds of paper choices and the results they achieve;
use a wide variety of illustration mediums;
create a well composed image through the practice of formal design principles;
execute quality draftsmanship and presentation skills.

rows.title: Advanced Watercolor Painting I
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:

continue to improve watercolor skills and techniques developed in 7A & 7B.
create a series of work based upon their own concepts and ideas;
utilize museums and galleries as a learning source.

rows.title: Introduction to Art
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: differentiate and apply art historical methodologies
identify visual elements and principles of design used in artwork
interpret and critique artwork using appropriate art historical terminology
tie form and function of artwork to medium and technique
analyze and discuss the role of art and artists in cultures across the globe

rows.title: Art History - Twentieth- and Twenty-First Century Art
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: identify and establish an argument for the cultural significance of, and historical values embodied in, artwork from the twentieth century;
identify and establish an argument for the cultural significance of, and historical values embodied in, artwork from the twenty-first century;
identify and establish an argument for the art style, cultural significance, and historical value of original artwork viewed in museums (in person or virtually).

rows.title: Survey of Art from Prehistory to the Medieval Era
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Identify, examine, and assess representative works of art and architecture from prehistory to the medieval era employing appropriate art historical terminology.
Analyze works of art and architecture in terms of aesthetic, socio-political, religious, historical, technological, and cultural contexts in which they were created.
Develop critical thinking, information literacy, and problem solving through an engagement with art, architecture, artists, and patrons from prehistory to the medieval era.

rows.title: Introduction to Astronomy: Stars and the Universe
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: review and explain the scientific method, as it applies to astronomy;
describe the Earth’s position in the universe by comparing the scale and structure of the solar system, galaxies and universe;
describe the relation between the seasons, constellations, and motion of the Earth about the sun;
demonstrate a basic knowledge of the nature of light as electromagnetic radiation;
demonstrate a basic knowledge of telescopes, spectrographs, and other astronomical tools;
describe the properties of our sun, including its structure, composition, and methods of energy production and transport;
describe and explain the relationship between energy production in the suns interior, and observable surface phenomena such as sunspots, flares, and magnetism;
demonstrate a basic knowledge of the age, type, composition, and evolution of stars;
identify the constituents and properties of the interstellar medium;
identify and describe the structure, contents, and dynamics of the Milky Way galaxy;
describe the large-scale structure and contents of the Universe;
describe and demonstrate understanding of competing cosmological models for the evolution of the universe, as well as contemporary evidence in support of each model;
demonstrate basic knowledge about the search for life beyond of the Earth, and recent developments in the search for extra solar planets;
identify at least 10 different seasonal constellations and bright stars, as well as planets currently visible in the night sky.

rows.title: Automotive Engines
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: verify and interpret engine concerns, and determine necessary action;
inspect an engine assembly for fuel, oil, coolant, and other leaks, and determine necessary action;
perform cooling system, cap, recovery system tests (pressure, combustion leakage, and temperature), and determine necessary action;
inspect, replace, and adjust drive belts, tensioners, and pulleys;
test coolant; drain and recover coolant; flush and refill cooling system with recommended coolant; bleed air as required;
inspect, test, remove, and replace engine cooling and heater system hoses, radiator, thermostat and housing, and water pump;
inspect, and test fans(s) (electrical or mechanical), fan clutch, fan shroud, and air dams;
inspect, test, and replace oil temperature and pressure switches and sensors;
Inspect oil pump gears or rotors, housing, pressure relief devices, and pump drive; perform necessary action;
diagnose engine noises and vibrations, and the cause of excessive oil consumption, unusual engine exhaust color, odor, and sound; determine necessary action;
visually inspect cylinder head(s) for cracks, check gasket surface areas for warpage and leakage;
install cylinder heads and gaskets, and tighten according to manufacturer’s specifications and procedures;
inspect and test valve springs for squareness, pressure, free-height comparison, valve spring retainers, locks, and valve grooves and replace as needed;
inspect valve guides for wear, check valve guide height, and stem to guide clearance, recondition or replace as needed;
check valve spring assembled height and valve stem height; service valve and spring assemblies as needed;
inspect pushrods, rocker arms, rocker arm pivots and shafts for wear, bending, cracks, looseness, and blocked oil passages (orifices), and perform necessary action;
adjust valves (mechanical and hydraulic lifters);
inspect and replace timing belt(s), overhead cam drive sprockets, and tensioners, check belt tension, and adjust as necessary;
verify camshaft(s) timing according to manufacturer’s specifications and procedures;
inspect camshaft drives (including gear wear and backlash, sprocket and chain wear); replace as necessary;
inspect camshaft for runout, journal wear and lobe wear;
establish camshaft(s) timing and cam sensor indexing according to manufacturer’s specifications and procedures;
disassemble engine block; clean and prepare components for inspection and reassembly;
inspect engine block for visible cracks, passage condition, core and gallery plug condition, surface warpage, and determine necessary action;
inspect and measure cylinder walls for damage/wear, deglaze and determine necessary action;

Inspect crankshaft for end play, straightness, journal damage, keyway damage, thrust flange and sealing surface condition, and visual surface cracks; check oil passage condition; measure journal wear; check crankshaft sensor reluctor ring (where applicable); determine necessary action;
Inspect and measure main and connecting rod bearings for damage, clearance, and end play; determine necessary action;
replace camshaft, main and connecting rod bearings using manufacturer’s recommended procedures;
inspect, measure, service pistons and pins, and install piston rings;
assemble the engine using gaskets, seals, and formed-in-place (tube-applied) sealants, thread sealers, etc., according to manufacturer’s specifications;
prime engine lubrication system;
confirm engine operation.

rows.title: Automotive Automatic Transmissions and Transaxles
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: identify and interpret transmission/transaxle concern, assure proper engine operation, and determine necessary action;
diagnose unusual fluid usage, level, and condition concerns, and determine necessary action;
perform pressure and stall tests, and determine necessary action;
perform lock up converter system tests, and determine necessary action;
diagnose electronic, mechanical, hydraulic, vacuum control system concerns, and determine necessary action;
diagnose transmission/transaxle gear reduction/multiplication concerns using driving, driven, and held member (power flow) principles;
inspect, adjust or replace throttle linkages or cables, and check gear select indicator (as applicable);
service transmission/transaxle, perform visual inspection; and replace fluids and filters;
inspect and replace external seals and gaskets;
inspect, leak test, flush, and replace cooler, lines, and fittings;
diagnose electronic transmission control systems using the appropriate tool; determine necessary action;
disassemble, clean, and inspect transmission/transaxle and reassemble;
check torque converter and transmission cooling system for contamination;
inspect, measure, and reseal oil pump assembly and components;
measure endplay or preload, and determine necessary action;
inspect, measure, and replace thrust washers. bearings and bushings;
inspect oil delivery seal rings, ring grooves, and sealing surface areas, roller and sprag clutch, races, rollers, sprags, springs, cages, and retainers, and determine necessary action;
inspect and measure planetary gear assembly, case bores, passages, bushings, vents, and mating surfaces and determine necessary action;
inspect transaxle drive, link chains, sprockets, gears, bearings, and bushings, and perform necessary action;
inspect, measure, repair, adjust or replace transaxle final drive components;
inspect clutch drum, piston, check balls, springs, retainers, seals, and friction and pressure plates, and replace as needed;
measure clutch pack clearance, and adjust as needed;
air test operation of clutch and servo assemblies;
inspect bands and drums; adjust or replace as needed.

rows.title: Automotive Manual Transmissions and Transaxles
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

inspect and replace drive axle shaft seals, bearings, and retainers;

disassemble, inspect, and reassemble transfer case and components.

describe fuel injection operation;
diagnose throttle body fuel injection systems;
diagnosis port fuel injection systems.

demonstrate basic strategies for both singles and doubles matches;
track their blood pressure;
recognize the symptoms of hypertension and pre-diabetes;

demonstrate increased strength, flexibility, agility, and cardiovascular fitness.

rows.title: Introduction to the Science of Biology
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: describe the scientific method and how it is used by scientists to further scientific knowledge;
cite the characteristics exhibited by all living things;
describe how a cell is structured and explain how it functions in terms of cell membrane phenomena, genetic control mechanisms, and cellular division;
explain the purpose, products, reactants, and major steps in photosynthesis and cellular respiration;
describe the structure of DNA, how it is replicated, the process of transcription, and the process of translation;
describe major environmental concern(s) of our modern world;
explain the Darwinian concept of evolution, as modified by modern scientific knowledge;
explain the factors that affect population density and growth rate;
map the relationship(s) between organisms within an ecosystem in relation to their niche and place in the food chain/web;
describe the mechanisms by which a trait can be inherited and expressed.

rows.title: Introduction to Public Health
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: define important foundational concepts in community/public health;
distinguish the difference between personal and public health and provide examples of each;

explain how public health programs differ from and serve as a compliment to traditional medical care. Include an analysis of the organization, financing and delivery of various medical and population-based services in the United States healthcare system;
describe the historical development of public health including the various disciplines, the local agencies, and the most important achievements of public health programs and policies;
outline strategies for prevention, detection and control of infectious and chronic disease;
identify the components of the Whole School, Whole Child, Whole Community (WSCC) model designed to improve learning and health in our nation's school;
outline the processes of community organizing and of health promotion programming;

analyze current public health issues and describe how they affect societal well-being in areas such as maternal, infant and child health; adolescent development; mental health; senior care; local health disparities; and abuse prevention;
describe the Dual Diagnosis/Co-Occurring Disorders approach to treating people who suffer from both an addiction and a psychiatric disorder;

describe the determinants of health (biological considerations, social factors, environmental conditions, behavioral and cultural factors, access to health services, and policy) and explain the role of each in determining local, national and global organization and policy; analyze proposals to alter those determinants;
demonstrate the use of basic epidemiological methods;
explain the inter-relationship between human beings and their environment as they relate to communicable diseases and the health of populations;
identify, assess, and utilize credible information resources on current public health issues;
identify common practices that contribute to intentional and unintentional workplace injuries and public health policies that would reduce their occurrences;
communicate orally and in writing in the scientific language of the discipline using credible resources.

rows.title: Principles of Animal Biology and Evolution
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:

Identify levels of biological organization ranging from cells to organisms and discuss their interdependencies;
Describe the general structure of cells of heterotrophic protists, fungi, and animals;
Identify structures of heterotrophic protists, fungi, and animals; and investigate how they obtain, manipulate, and utilize materials and energy for growth, maintenance, reproduction and development;
Explain the principles and mechanisms of evolution and relate them to the systematics of animals, fungi, and heterotrophic protists;
Relate population genetics to evolution and the diversity of life;
Analyze interactions and changes that occur among organisms and the environment and discuss social systems and behavior.

list levels of organization with emphasis on the structure of cells through interacting organ systems and explain how higher levels depend on lower levels for each system;
identify and describe:
-gross anatomy and location of organs,
-histology of organs,
-systemic functions,
-functions of component organs and how each contributes to the systemic function;
explain how the systemic functions interact with each other within the human organism;
describe the events of embryonic and fetal development and the anatomy of extra-embryonic membranes;
maintain a safe laboratory environment;
demonstrate proper use of microscopes and dissection techniques.

rows.title: Human Heredity and Evolution

relate genetic principles to population genetics and evolution;
