analyze and articulate the concepts of race and racism, the racialization process, eurocentrism, and white supremacy in addition to the competing forces of self-determination, liberation, anti-racism and decolonization and how these forces shape and explain the historical and cultural experiences of early Asian Americans in the United States;
critique the Master Narrative of U.S. history and view major historical events from the perspective of Asian Americans;

examine push and pull reasons for overall immigration and settlement patterns, including transnational immigration;
examine major federal, state, and local governments and their policies that impacted the civil rights of Asian Americans prior to 1945;

analyze the influence of Anti-Asian sentiment on immigration laws, school segregation, and local, state, and federal level laws involving Asian Americans;
appraise the significance of Asian American Civil Rights Movements and/or other social movements that Asian Americans were a part of;
identify the impact of international relations on domestic policies affecting Asian Americans, including the case of WWII and mass incarceration of Japanese Americans;

analyze the impact of U.S. wars and militarism on women in Asia;

rows.title: Futsal
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate the rules of Futsal;
demonstrate basic Futsal passing skills in a drill and game situation;
demonstrate ability to play in a small sided Futsal game.

rows.title: Global Environmental Solutions
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Analyze approaches to environmental studies and sustainability of ecosystems and natural resources;
Understand cultural traditions in land-use ethics and indigenous peoples rights and relationships to nature;
Evaluate the historical stages in the emergence of conservation and environmental movements and environmental action today;
Assess how political processes in the United States interact with environmental change, and how they influence public policies and regulations regarding the environment;
Evaluate the most significant changes occurring in recent decades in the atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere, and biosphere and analyze sustainable problem solving to these changes around the globe;
Evaluate the impacts of individual, community, regional, and global actions and movements.

rows.title: Introduction to Physical Geography Laboratory
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: apply observational, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills through analytical viewing, writing, and quantitative techniques which demonstrate understanding of the processes that produce patterns on the landscape;
measure, interpret, and analyze spatial data on maps, aerial photographs, and satellite imagery;
synthesize and integrate various forms of spatial data in geographic information systems;
apply geographic computer simulations/models to the analysis of spatial interactions, distributions, and relationships;
apply selected meteorological techniques and tools to the observation, measurement, analysis, and portrayal of weather data;
identify, classify, map, or perform other laboratory/field activities which demonstrate the properties and/or spatial covariation of selected climate, soil, and vegetation types;
classify and identify properties of the most common earth materials;
apply map/image analysis techniques to identify and explain selected landform types, their associated erosional and depositional features, and land use patterns;
recognize his/her awareness of local and regional atmospheric, fluvial, coastal, and tectonic processes/hazards.

rows.title: Spatial Analysis with GIS
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: define the data model structure of cell-based grid modeling;
generate cell-based grids from point data distributions;
operate the spatial analysis tools in a desktop GIS system;
create continuous surface (isoline) maps from themes in discrete grids;
apply techniques of spatial referencing, surface shaping, and address geocoding;
produce 3-D surface models from grids of Z-value magnitude data;
perform analyses of zonal and neighborhood distributions;
convert thematic data between vector and raster formats;
select map projections appropriate to map scales and presentation purposes;
overlay accurately raster-based image data with thematic vector data by means of registration and rectification utilities in GIS software;
perform viewshed analysis and map view planes in urban regions;
demonstrate competency in methods of representing spatial information through the production of maps, charts, and diagrams.

rows.title: World Regional Geography
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate an awareness of the major regions of the world, and significant places and patterns within those regions
identify absolute and relative locations of significant places;
identify major current trends in the region’s political economy, cultural evolution, and environmental issues;
compare and contrast regions based on their physical, political, economic, and social characteristics as evidenced in their cultural landscapes;
identify regions and major sub-regions on thematic maps and interpret information from them about the spatial distribution of phenomena;
identify major map types and the appropriateness of their use in presenting geographic information.
demonstrate knowledge of major geographic issues and trends in the contemporary world
identify on maps major physiographic divisions of the continents;
distinguish developed and developing regions and nations based on economic, political, and social indicators;
identify types of globalization trends and processes operating on the global scale using spatial indicators;
compare and contrast population distributions and growth/implosion trends among regions and major representative countries;
recognize the forces of diversity and ethnic identity at work in regions that counter globalization trends and cause devolution;
compare the status of indigenous peoples, women, and minority populations in regional cultural context;
articulate the attributes of culture that commonly distinguish cultural regions: language, religion, ethnicity, traditions, and social relations;

identify global environmental change concerns and trends in the inter-regional context of the strongly interconnected Earth system: global warming, land degradation, air and water quality, and natural hazards;
evaluate different approaches to regional study and methods of geographic observation.

rows.title: Physical Geology
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: explain the scientific method;
explain, discuss, analyze, identify and/or interpret the fundamental concepts, principles, and interactions of Earth’s systems applicable to the Geological Sciences;
apply, explain, discuss, analyze, identify and/or interpret the internal and external processes that shape and form the Earth;
apply, explain and/or discuss the rock cycle and identify and describe the basic properties of rocks and minerals;
explain, discuss, analyze, identify and/or interpret the fundamentals, and ramifications, of plate tectonics and Earth’s resources;
explain, discuss, analyze, identify and/or interpret, how geological environments are formed, changed and eroded through geological time;
communicate complex course concepts effectively in writing and diagrams and apply critical thinking and problem solving skills to make informed decisions in life.

rows.title: Historical Geology
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Apply the principles of the scientific method to analyze geologic data and synthesize testable hypotheses about geologic sequences.

Analyze and explain relationships between key concepts that have helped build knowledge, hypotheses and theories in Historical Geology. These key concepts can include: Fossilization; Ecology, Evolution and Extinction; Plate Tectonics; Geologic Time and Dating Methods; The Supercontinent Cycle and Paleo-Climate;
Apply knowledge of common rocks and minerals to infer the conditions and geologic setting in which they are formed.

Apply knowledge of common fossils, their formation and place in the geologic record to explaining evidence for evolution of life, including processes such as natural selection and the effects of climate change on life on Earth.

Synthesize knowledge of plate tectonic processes and regimes to evaluate its role in major geologic events in Earth's history, such as extinctions, episodes of global cooling or warming, the rise of oxygen.

rows.title: The Planets
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Describe physical and chemical properties of the Sun, planets, asteroid and comets.
Describe theories of planetary formation in our solar system;
Describe the compositional differences among rocky planets, gas giants and ice giants in our solar system;
Identify and explain major planetary analog sites on Earth.

rows.title: History of Western Civilization Since 1600
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to interpret primary and secondary sources and to compose an argument which uses them, as appropriate, for support;
Analyze the concept of the West;
Demonstrate an understanding of Western Civilization through multiple analytical categories such as race, class, gender and ethnicity;
Explain the historical significance of developments in science, and new discoveries and inventions;
Show the historical significance of developments in cultural areas such as art, music, architecture and religion;
Analyze social organization, economic organization, and political ideological trends in the western world, and explain their historical significance;
Analyze the relevance of history in today's world.

rows.title: Colonial Latin America
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate critical thinking and analytical skills by utilizing methods of inquiry used by historians;
recognize the significance of primary and secondary sources and how to interpret them appropriately;
integrate geographical knowledge with cultural and historical knowledge to assess the development of an emerging Latin America;

examine, evaluate, and discuss the experiences, roles, achievements, and contributions of Indigenous and African people in Latin America from the Pre-Columbian era to the 19th-century struggles for independence;
closely examine the role of women, including their struggle for equality, within the context of an emerging Latin American;
closely examine the role of Africans, including their struggle for equality, within the context of an emerging Latin America;
assess the historical roots of racism and patriarchy, and the impact on ethnic conflict in Latin America;
examine and evaluate European colonial, social, political, economic, and cultural institutions in the shaping of Indigenous, Black, Mestizo, and Mulatto communities in Latin America.

rows.title: Asian American History: 18th Century to 1945
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Critically analyze the intersection of race and racism as they relate to class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability, tribal citizenship, sovereignty, language, and/or age in Asian American communities and other communities of color;

Critically review how struggle, resistance, racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and enacted by Asian Americans and other communities of color are relevant to current and structural issues such as communal, national, international, and transnational politics as, for example, in immigration, reparations, settler-colonialism, multiculturalism, language policies.

analyze and articulate the concepts of race and racism, the racialization process, eurocentrism, and white supremacy in addition to the competing forces of self-determination, liberation, anti-racism and decolonization and how these forces shape and explain the historical and cultural experiences of early Asian Americans in the United States;
critique the Master Narrative of U.S. history and view major historical events from the perspective of Asian Americans;
analyze the origins of the U.S. political system and United States Constitution including the efforts of Asian Americans to gain citizenship and civil rights;
analyze the political perspective of the authors of the Constitution;
discuss the definition of citizenship and how it has changed over time under the U.S. Constitution and federal and state laws;
assess the impact of the U.S. Constitution on immigration and citizenship policies which excluded and shaped the early Asian American population;
compare and contrast the relationship and features between the California Constitution, U.S. Constitution, and federal, state, and local court decisions that impacted Asian Americans;

evaluate the historical experiences of Asian Americans, their interaction with federal, state and local governments and compare with other major racial/ethnic groups (African Americans, American Indians, European Americans, Latinx);
identify the contributions of Asian immigrants to the development of U.S. society and institutions;
analyze the impact of Orientalism on European and US imperialism, colonialism, wars and US militarism in Asia;
examine push and pull reasons for overall immigration and settlement patterns, including transnational immigration;
examine major federal, state, and local governments and their policies that impacted the civil rights of Asian Americans prior to 1945;
compare and contrast labor, the development of unions, and workers movements involving Asian Americans;
analyze the influence of Anti-Asian sentiment on immigration laws, school segregation, and local, state, and federal level laws involving Asian Americans;
appraise the significance of Asian American Civil Rights Movements and/or other social movements that Asian Americans were a part of;
identify the impact of international relations on domestic policies affecting Asian Americans, including the case of WWII and mass incarceration of Japanese Americans;
examine a range of primary and secondary sources such as oral histories, court rulings, newspaper articles, memoirs, poems, political cartoons, and other visual media;
analyze the impact of U.S. wars and militarism on women in Asia;

rows.title: U.S. Women's History Post-Reconstruction
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: evaluate the significant political, social and economic events of modern American history from 1877 to the present from a woman's perspective and relate the impact of these events on women;
demonstrate an understanding of how women influenced modern American history from the late nineteenth century to the present;
study the lives of women in different geographic regions of the U. S. and explain how regional differences shaped women's opportunities;
demonstrate an awareness of diversity of experiences among women while noting the interconnections among the various institutions that shape women's lives in modern American history;
examine significant Constitutional issues and Supreme Court cases since 1877, especially as these relate to women;
explain the impact of major foreign policy issues and debates from 1877 to the present upon women and society;
analyze political reform movements of the nineteenth, twentieth and twenty-first centuries especially as they relate to women;
describe the development of California politics from 1877 to the present, with special focus on state and local politics and legislation, as they relate to women;
explain, in relation to women, economic change, social change, and the importance of science and technology in America's development;
analyze the Constitution of the State of California and amendments that impact citizenship and voting rights;
describe the effects of growth and power of federal government upon women, and how these changes impacted federal state relations between 1877 and the present.

rows.title: The African-American Experience in U.S. History Through the Civil War
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: analyze and articulate concepts such as race and racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, ethno-centrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, decolonization, sovereignty, imperialism, settler colonialism, and anti-racism as analyzed in any one or more of the following: Native American Studies, African American Studies, Asian American Studies, and Latina and Latino American Studies.

critically analyze the intersection of race and racism as they relate to class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability, tribal citizenship, sovereignty, language, and/or age in Native American, African American, Asian American, and/or Latina and Latino American communities.

critically review how struggle, resistance, racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and enacted by Native Americans, African Americans, Asian Americans and/or Latina and Latino Americans are relevant to current and structural issues such as communal, national, international, and transnational politics as, for example, in immigration, reparations, settler-colonialism, multiculturalism, language policies.
identify the origins of African-American history as a field of academic investigation and study;
identify and analyze historic anti-racist struggles engaged in by African Americans and their connection to present-day social, economic, political and cultural policies and practices;
explain the nature and impact of different European peoples’ early relationship to West African societies;
trace the founding of the American colonies and their different relationships to African slavery;
compare the complex relationship between Native Americans, Euro-Americans and African-Americans during the colonial period;
analyze the evolving role race and racism plays in the institutionalization of slavery;
explain the significance of the American Revolution and African-American participation in it;
analyze the origins of the U.S. political system and the United States Constitution including the anti-racist efforts of African-Americans to gain freedom and political equality;
discuss the political philosophies of the framers of the Constitution;
analyze the Constitutional debate concerning slavery and the role that African-Americans should play in the nation;
discuss the implication of the dislocation of Native Americans, the rise of cotton and the expansion of slavery in the South;
describe the distinctive development of Northern states and free African-American communities in them;
explain the abolitionist movement and its evolution from moral activism to political activism;

discuss how citizenship (with its concomitant rights and obligations) comes to be defined and how African-Americans and their allies, at both state and federal levels, struggle to expand that definition through protest and changes in state and federal Constitutions.

explain territorial expansion, its impact on Native American, Asian Americans, and Mexican and Mexican American populations and, in particular the issue of California statehood and the state’s constitution, and the controversy of slavery;
trace the political dissension between the North and the South and the Constitutional crisis which results in secession and the beginning of the Civil War;
describe the war, African-American participation in it and the efforts by slaves to seize their freedom;
compare and analyze both presidential and congressional Reconstruction and the political, economic, and social consequences of their missions.

rows.title: United States History since 1865
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to interpret primary and secondary sources and to compose an
argument which uses supportive evidence;
Demonstrate an understanding of U.S. History through analytical categories such as race,
class, gender, sexuality, and ethnicity;
Analyze economic, political, and cultural developments as well as social movements and
assess their historical significance;
Analyze the relevance of Modern American History to the present day;

explain the causes of the expansion of industrial capitalism, economic transformations of the 20th century, and analyze the effects of economic changes, major social and cultural developments, and their effects on women, gender roles, working class relations, racial/ethnic minority groups, U.S diplomacy, and their historical significance;

demonstrate an understanding of the crisscrossing dynamics of race, ethnicity, gender, religion, class and other analytical categories in American society, and assess the impact of these dynamics on U.S. political institutions, laws, and electoral politics;

outline and discuss contributions and experiences of racial/ethnic, gender, and social groups in the development of U.S. political, economic, cultural and social institutions; discuss interactions among these groups; evaluate the role of geography in the context of economic and political change;
identify and analyze the major periods of social change from Reconstruction to the present; evaluate the roots of reform and any long-term consequences for U.S. society;
trace the evolution of U.S. foreign policy and its impact on U.S. society and the world;
discuss the power and limitations of federal court decisions in advancing civil rights of women, racial and ethnic minorities, and gender groups, and in redefining citizens' due process rights,
evaluate 20th Century amendments to the California state Constitution and state legislation which have had a significant impact on both California and national policies;
demonstrate an understanding of America's geographic growth, and growing influence and power, in global context;
explain the major economic, technological and scientific developments and their historical significance;
identify and analyze the major trends in politics, political attitudes and conflicts, through both mainstream events and reform movements, and explain their historical significance;
analyze the relevance of history in today's world;
demonstrate the ability to interpret primary and secondary sources and to compose an argument which uses them, as appropriate, for support.

rows.title: Introduction to ICD Coding
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: explain the historical development of ICD systems;
differentiate between nomenclature and classification and show how they complement each other;
explain the structure and purpose of ICD-10-CM;
discuss the coding conventions, symbols and abbreviations used in ICD-10-CM;
apply diagnosis codes according to current guidelines;
analyze the accuracy of diagnostic coding;
analyze the documentation in the health record to ensure it supports the diagnosis and reflects the patient’s progress, and clinical findings;
assess ethical standards of practice;
appropriately use medical and coding references, such as; Merck Manual, AHA Coding Clinic, Official ICD-10-CM Guidelines for Coding and Reporting, and others.

rows.title: Legal and Ethical Aspects of Healthcare
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: apply healthcare legal terminology;
identify the use of legal documents for patient care and the protection of health information;
apply legal concepts and principles of the practice of health information management;
apply confidentiality, privacy and security measures, and policies and procedures, for internal and external use and exchange to protected electronic health information;
apply retention and destruction policies for health information;
apply system security policies according to departmental and organizational data/information standards;
apply policies and procedures surrounding issues of access and disclosure of protected health information;
describe software used in the completion of HIM processes for release of information;
analyze policies and procedures to ensure organizational compliance with regulations and standards;
comply with ethical standards of practice.

rows.title: Medical Coding 2
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: apply basic diagnosis and procedure coding processes using Current Procedural Terminology (CPT), International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10-CM) and Healthcare Common Procedural Coding System (HCPCS) manuals;

apply conventions, symbols, and abbreviations used inCurrent Procedural Terminology (CPT), International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10-CM) and Healthcare Common Procedural Coding System (HCPCS) manuals;
apply the coding rules and guidelines to actual diagnostic and operative coding problems;
identify appropriate codes using Current Procedural Terminology (CPT), International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10-CM) and Healthcare Common Procedural Coding System (HCPCS) coding books;
identify medical record documentation used to support the coding process;
collect coded data required for data abstracting and reporting purposes;
utilize software in the completion of health information management processes for coding and data collection;
apply the coding and sequencing principles of International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10-CM) to assign the correct codes to medical record scenarios and case studies;
evaluate the accuracy of diagnostic and procedural coding;
apply policies and procedures for the use of data required in healthcare reimbursement;
identify discrepancies between supporting documentation and coded data;
develop appropriate physician queries to resolve data and coding discrepancies;
describe the various other nomenclatures and classification.

rows.title: Women and Health
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

outcomes: identify 3 major events leading to the women’s health movement;
list 5 actions for becoming a responsible health consumer;
research family roots to explore genetic and lifestyle choices that influence present and future health;
identify steps for personal health care;
analyze the socio-cultural influences on the image of women ;
identify 1 challenge and 1 opportunity for each major life transition;
identify 5 characteristics of a healthy relationship;
identify and evaluate current reproductive choices;
develop strategies for maintaining a healthy lifestyle in 1 of the following areas:
eating or exercise patterns
stress management
substance use and misuse
identify risks and explain steps for prevention of major chronic conditions that impact women;
list and explain 3 examples of protective legislation and 3 resources for women.

rows.title: Advanced Medical Terminology and Disease Process
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: describe structural organization of the human body;
identify body systems and describe normal functions of each system;
identify common pathology related to each system;
analyze pathology as it relates to the interaction of body systems;
discuss the implications of disease and disability when homeostasis is not maintained;
describe the implications for treatment related to pathology;
compare body structure and function of the human body across the lifespan to include developmental, congenital, and childhood diseases and disorders;
identify the various mechanisms of disease; diagnosis and treatment;
describe the role of nutrition and metabolism in health and disease;
describe hereditary diseases;
identify the pathogenesis, clinical manifestations and therapeutic modalities as they relate to diseases of each body system.

rows.title: Guts and Butts Workout
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:

assess and measure strength and flexibility of hip, thigh and abdominal areas;
demonstrate correct strengthening and flexibility movements for the entire body;
track their blood pressure;
identify problem foods as they relate to diabetes and hypertension;
waist to hip ratio and its relationship to diabetes and hypertension;
demonstrate correct body alignment.

rows.title: World Mythology
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Discuss and identify classic approaches to why mythology arises;
Discuss and identify archetypes, including character; symbol; and plot;
Discuss ritual theory and identify examples in narratives;
Discuss and identify aspects of religion within a narrative;
Discuss and identify various forms of narrative;
Discuss and identify sacred spaces within narratives;
Discuss and identify aspects of symbol and language;
Discuss and identify aspects of cultural appropriation, both positive and negative.

rows.title: Residential Space Planning

explain the demands that group activities place on space relationships;
plan for both group and private space;
design functional work areas relating to food preparation, hygiene, and storage;
articulate the principles relating to lighting, heating, and ventilating;
draw floor plans and elevations;
use color in space planning.

rows.title: Principles of Interior Design
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

demonstrate an understanding of how personality and mood are affected by color and texture;
demonstrate the ability to perceive how hues, value and intensity affect the surroundings;
show an understanding of the way shapes and forms are interrelated;
merge colors and textures to attain harmony and variety with interior spaces;
show an understanding of the way colors and textures were used during different times in history.

rows.title: Fundamentals of Lighting
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: evaluate existing commercial and residential lighting installations;
design a lighting system for a residential and commercial establishment using drafting equipment;
discuss how artificial and natural light can be used to render color;
describe the relationship between direct, indirect, task, ambient, general, specific, and accent light;
describe the function of various luminaries;

discuss the effect of Title 24 on commercial lighting design;
read reflective ceiling plans including the use of electrical symbols and lettering
develop local sources for obtaining further lighting knowledge and products;
develop a lighting proposal for a client, including landscape lighting;
use lighting as a creative medium.

select materials, finishes, appliances, and cabinetry which can be used to complete the
design;
use a NKBA Professional Resource Library to depict the kitchen and bath;
calculate the cost to the clients of constructing the kitchen and bath;

designer and client;
apply the current California Title XXIV Lighting Code;
use colors used in universal design.

rows.title: Introduction to Micro, Nano, and Semiconductor Manufacturing

compare and contrast the classes of clean rooms and the operating procedures unique to each class;

perform scalar measurements from scanning electron microscope images.

understand the concept of ratio and solve proportions;
understand numerical trigonometry, polar coordinates, and perform elementary calculations;
be able to perform conversions between English and metric measurements;
apply the above to problems from diverse technical fields.

rows.title: Intermediate Japanese

demonstrate an greater command and fluency of the language;
demonstrate improvement in speaking skills beyond the elementary level;
develop the vocabulary and grammar at the intermediate level to express in more details their opinions and experiences;

produce texts such as essays and diary entries at the intermediate level;
demonstrate an understanding of the intricacy of social and cultural components of Japan;
read, comprehend, and be able to analyze a variety of passages of medium difficulty.

rows.title: Japanese Conversation and Culture II
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

increase the pronunciation and sentence intonation skills;
narrate, describe, and explain not only current but also past activities;
carry on a conversation in Japanese on topics studied by applying their knowledge of vocabulary and idiomatic expressions;
demonstrate reading and writing ability of the hiragana, Japanese phonetic characters;
demonstrate a deeper understanding and appreciation of the culture, the geography, and the history of the Japanese-speaking people.

rows.title: Beginning Judo

demonstrate physical development in (Renshindo) and mental development (Shushindo);
demonstrate an improvement in neuromuscular development and mental discipline;

track their blood pressure;
identify metabolic syndrome.

demonstrate the approved/ accepted mechanics & signals;

conduct harmonic analyses of musical examples that contain 5/3, 6/3, and 6/4 techniques, sequences, melodic and rhythmic figuration, leading-tone 7th chords, mixture, diatonic applied dominants, and diatonic modulation;

realize figured bass lines that indicate the use of 5/3, 6/3, and 6/4 techniques, sequences, melodic and rhythmic figuration, leading-tone 7th chords, mixture, diatonic applied dominants, and diatonic modulation;

value the music as a form of self expression through creativity and cultural influences;
explain the similarities and differences between spirituals, gospel music and the blues;
understand the importance of design and form in music in regard to structure;
have improved their listening ability and sensitivity to the various jazz styles through informed listening and analysis;
identify major Jazz artists.

rows.title: Basic Music Skills

develop simple and compound meters;
identify basic properties of sound;
show understanding of intervals;
identify key signatures;
construct scales;
explain what diatonic chords are.

rows.title: Jazz Combo

develop recognition of exotic scales;
demonstrate melody harmonization;
develop recognition and construction of chords;
demonstrate knowledge of standard and substitute chord changes;
demonstrate chord re-harmonization;
construct scales used for jazz improvisation in Major keys;
construct scales used for jazz improvisation in Minor keys;
demonstrate practical application in small group performance.

rows.title: Jazz Ensemble
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

demonstrate a comprehension of various jazz styles;
demonstrate the ability to perform characteristics appropriate to jazz styles;
demonstrate knowledge of musicals elements intonation, dynamics and expression;
demonstrate awareness of individual responsibility to the success of ensemble performance;
demonstrate rehearsal techniques and performance conduct.

rows.title: Chamber Winds
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

describe an understanding of ensemble technique, validity of style, shadings of interpretation;
critically evaluate and rehearse various types of repertoire for the purpose of performance.

rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate familiarity with musical productions literature;
demonstrate proficiency on their instruments;
strategically rehearse and perform works.

rows.title: Mental Health Nursing
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate awareness of mental health stigma, health disparities, and access barriers in vulnerable populations;
care for the client experiencing psychiatric illnesses with unpredictable outcomes;
identify alterations in body image, such as eating disorders;
identify principles involved in the physiological care of the client with addictions and the effects of addictions on psychosocial behaviors;
verbalize the care needed by the suicidal client;
describe the management of clients with personality disorders;
describe techniques for intervening with angry, aggressive, manipulative, or impulsive clients;
demonstrate techniques of therapeutic communication in groups and with individuals experiencing illnesses with unpredictable outcomes;
discuss the application of principles of group dynamics in health care;
compare and contrast the differences in the care of the client with an alteration in thought processes including psychoses, dementias, and delirium;
evaluate the effects of severe or panic levels of anxiety on the client response to interpersonal situations and physical conditions;
discuss crisis intervention;
discuss pharmacological interventions in psychiatric conditions manifested by:
psychoses
anxiety
depression
addictions
mania
personality disorders;
use the self as a therapeutic agent in the delivery of health care;
implement the nursing process in the care of clients with the following nursing diagnoses:
sensory/perceptual alteration
altered thought processes
anxiety
alteration in nutrition
sleep pattern disturbance
impaired social interaction
ineffective individual coping
memory, impaired
risk for injury
risk of violence: self/others
social isolation
pain, acute or chronic
self-care deficit;
identify and describe psychosocial concerns common to the elderly client;
identify precipitating causes, symptoms and collaborative management of the elder who has been abused;
discuss the causes, symptoms and collaborative management of clients with dementia;
adapt health teaching to special needs of the aging client;
discuss legal-ethical concepts as they relate to clients in psychiatric settings.

rows.title: Adult Health II
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Theoretical:
identify and describe scientific principles that form the basis for assessments and nursing interventions which assist clients in adaptation to:
musculoskeletal dysfunction;
acute and chronic neurological dysfunction;
cardiovascular system dysfunction;
acute respiratory failure;
hematological disorders;
pancreatic and biliary dysfunction;
genitourinary disorders;
shock syndromes;
trauma to integument (burns);
disaster and triage management;
organ transplanttion;
Clinical:

application of the integrated theoretical framework that combines the Clinical Judgment Measurement Model (CJMM) and the Nursing Process in the formulation of nursing care plans for clients with nursing diagnoses of:
alteration in tissue perfusion;
gas exchange, impaired;
impaired physical mobility;
sensory-perceptual alteration;
urinary elimination, altered patterns;
activity intolerance;
sexual dysfunction;
decreased cardiac output;
fluid volume deficit/excess;
post-trauma syndrome;
collaborate with the client, family, and staff in developing a teaching plan for client's identified knowledge deficits;
discuss specific nutritional recommendations for the client who has disorders of the hepatobiliary system;
discuss specific nutritional recommendations for the client who has disorders of the renal system;
successfully demonstrate the following nursing skills:
nursing assessments: cardiovascular, neurological;
administration of oxygen;
tracheostomy care and suctioning;
chest tubes: assisting with insertion and removal, care of tubes and related assessments;
administration of blood components;
administration of intravenous medications by central and implanted venous access devices;
assistance with diagnostic tests utilized for clients with disorders outlined in theoretical outcomes;
plan and prioritize care for multiple patients in the acute setting;
care for the geriatric client identifying normal changes with aging.

rows.title: Clinical Skills Practice and Assessment Lab
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate mastery of theory application by performing at or above program percentile on benchmark exams;
demonstrate skills learned in the fundamentals of nursing course and Adult Health I, to include IV therapy, medication administration, tube feeding, and assessment;
demonstrate skills learned in the maternal newborn course to include assessment of the mother and newborn, Foley catheter insertion, Leopold's maneuver;
demonstrate skills learned in the pediatric nursing course to include IV skills, administration of safe dose of medication;
demonstrate how to administer medications understanding the concepts of pharmacology.

rows.title: Weight Management for Healthy Aging
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Name the classes of essential nutrients, their major functions and richest food sources;
identify the essential macronutrients and describe their impact on energy balance within the body;
identify the micronutrients, its richest sources and their effect in the body;
examine the energy systems functioning during rest and during different periods of physical activity;
identify the major concepts presented in the Dietary Reference Intakes, and the Dietary Guidelines for Americans to meet health and fitness needs;
identify nutrients of concern during the aging process;
study of diseases associated with aging and lifestyle, maintenance and preventative measures;
study fitness guidelines to promote health;
evaluate the connections between healthy diets and emotional wellness;
assess caloric nutritional intake in relation to current activity level;
flexibility, resistance and cardiovascular training to optimize weight loss and lifelong fitness.

rows.title: Nutrition for Healthy Living
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Identify the six classes of nutrients and their major roles in the body;
describe the dimensions of health and how they relate to nutrition;
analyze the reliability and safety of nutritional advice, resources, and products;
examine dietary guidelines and recommendations over the life span;
correlate the relationship between food influences, eating behavior, and health status;
analyze diet for nutritional adequacy and propose modifications to reduce disease risk and promote health.

rows.title: Contact Lens
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: cite major landmarks in contact lens development;
define terminology related to eyes and contact lenses;
describe various contact lens materials available for proper fit;
explain effects of wearing contact lenses, and indications and contradictions for fitting rigid and soft contact lenses;
describe various techniques to insert and remove contact lenses;
explain the use of contact lens solutions, care procedures, wearing schedules and follow-up eye exam appointments;
discuss the instruments used for the verification and modification of lenses;
describe how refractive surgical procedures affect contact lens fitters and state laws regarding contact lenses.

rows.title: Symbolic Logic
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate understanding of the concept of and criteria for deductive validity;
translate or symbolize natural language (e.g., ordinary English) into the languages of sentential and predicate logic and vice versa;
construct and evaluate sentential logic truth tables;
employ formal techniques for determining the invalidity of arguments in predicate logic;
construct proofs using natural deduction rules of sentential and predicate logic.

rows.title: Social and Political Philosophy
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Employ the methods of philosophical inquiry, especially the principles of logic and critical thinking to reason clearly, consistently, and carefully about ethics;
Employ the methods of philosophical inquiry to unmask and question assumptions and highlight distinctions;
Employ the methods of philosophical inquiry to hone the portable language skills of speaking and writing clearly and effectively, as well as listening and reading carefully and critically;

Employ the methods of philosophical inquiry to cultivate philosophical virtues of being open-minded, curious, free-thinking, imaginative, truth-seeking, appropriately skeptical, and intellectually humble and charitable;
Convey understanding of theories of justice, ethics, and human nature according to Plato and Aristotle;
Convey understanding of theories of justice, ethics, fairness, and rights according to utilitarians like Mill and Bentham and deontologists like Kant;
Convey understanding of theories of fairness, rights, and human nature according to Hobbes and egoists;
Explicate and analyze foundational social and political theories and ideas, including democracy and social contract theory;
Explicate and analyze foundational social and political theories and ideas, including liberalism, conservatism, capitalism, and socialism;
Explicate and analyze foundational social and political theories including authoritarianism, libertarianism, anarchism, neo-Marxism, and postmodernism. (Optional)

Explicate and analyze foundational social and political theories and apply them to at least two of the following contemporary issues: race and affirmative action; terrorism, torture, and surveillance; welfare, poverty, hunger, and wealth inequality; prostitution and pornography; free speech, hate speech, and censorship; technology, artificial intelligence, and piracy; offensive humor, trigger warnings, and cancel culture;
Convey understanding of the major social and political philosophical theories, arguments, and concepts expressed by Plato or Aristotle;
Convey understanding of the major social and political philosophical theories, arguments, and concepts expressed by Hobbes;
Convey understanding of the major social and political philosophical theories, arguments, and concepts expressed by at least two of the following: Locke, Rousseau, and Rawls;
Convey understanding of the major social and political philosophical theories, arguments, and concepts expressed by Confucius, Lao Tzu, Augustine, Machiavelli, Marx, and Arendt. (Optional)

rows.title: History of Photography
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate an understanding of 19th century photography as it relates to technological, historical and artistic issues;
identify photographs by their technical process;
demonstrate an understanding of 20th century photography as it relates to technological, historical and artistic issues;
demonstrate an understanding of photography's influence on the development of other arts;
assess the role of photography in their own lives;
identify the major themes and purposes of photography and articulate how these relate to photography's dual role as information technology and art;
interpret the various ways in which photographs have been used as vehicles of expression;
demonstrate an understanding of photography's most current manifestations;
identify and discuss non-western European photographic practices.

hand process images using cyanotype chemistry;
hand process images using van dyke brown chemistry;

using alternative process to work with fabric, textiles and three dimensional art;
Familiarity with historical processes, photographers, and movements and the influence on contemporary photography.

rows.title: Advanced Studio Lighting: Portraiture

advanced use and maintenance of studio strobes, power packs, hot lights, and monolights for portrait photography in the studio and on-location;

rows.title: Advanced Color Photography Methods

use advanced color relationships in digital photographs to create aesthetically complete compositions;

digitally manage color for creative compositions and accurate color profiles from capture to print;
control value, hue, intensity, and color temperature of a photograph with artificial lighting techniques;
understand how to create color mixtures and color relationships using artificial light sources;
make individual aesthetic decisions and judgements related to the the aesthetic and technical use of color in photography;
skillfully use a variety of advanced digital color techniques, tools, and materials;
independently produce a finished printed portfolio of digital color photographs that demonstrate advanced understanding of color theory and color management for photographic production;
critically analyze and discuss digital color photographs using advanced concepts and terminology for color theory principles and techniques;

production;
optimize image quality for a variety of outputs to store, transfer, and prepare
images for electronic and print presentation;
use, manipulate and composite images from a variety of sources into an artistic composition;

rows.title: General Physics I
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

addition, subtraction, dot product and cross product of vectors;
linear and rotational kinematics;
dynamics;
momentum;
work, kinetic energy, and potential energy;
rotational kinematics and dynamics;
statics;
gravitation.
operate standard laboratory equipment;
analyze laboratory data;
write comprehensive laboratory reports according to published lab report standards.

rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

special relativity;
quantum physics;
wave mechanics;
atomic physics;
solid state physics;
nuclear physics;
particle physics;
astrophysics and cosmology.

rows.title: Physics for Scientists and Engineers: Electromagnetism
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Analyze simple static charge distributions and calculate the resulting electric field and electric potential;
Analyze simple current distributions and calculate the resulting magnetic field;
Explain the physical location and motions of charged particles within objects in the presence of an electric or magnetic field;
Predict the trajectory of charged particles in uniform electric and magnetic fields;
Analyze situations in which the electric or magnetic field is changing in time using Faraday’s Law and/or Maxwell’s equations;
Analyze DC and AC circuits in terms of current, potential difference, and power dissipation for each element;
Design, perform, analyze, and assess the effectiveness of simple experiments to demonstrate physical phenomena;
Operate standard laboratory equipment and analysis tools, including digital data acquisition systems, spreadsheet programs, and plotting programs;
Analyze real-world experimental data, including appropriate use of units and significant figures;
Relate the results of experimental data to the physical concepts discussed in the lecture portion of the class.

rows.title: Introduction to Paralegal Studies
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: define the role of the paralegal within the legal profession;
identify and explain the fundamental skills needed for legal assisting/paralegalism;
explain and analyze the development, implementation, and enforcement processes of the American legal system;
explain and analyze the development, implementation, and enforcement processes of public policy at the state and local level;
describe the jurisdiction of various courts in the American judicial system, including state, federal and appellate courts;
explain how the civil process works;
explain how the criminal process works;
identify and explain the meaning and relative importance in the American legal system of constitutional law, statutory law, administrative law, and case law;
explain the requirements that must be met before a lawsuit can be brought in a particular court by a specific party;
discuss and analyze basic matters of substantive law;
identify and explain how to conduct valid, timely and relevant legal research;

Describe legal software systems frequently used by paralegals.
Practice using various legal software systems, including email, word processing, spreadsheets, PowerPoint presentations, database management systems, and timekeeping and billing.
Describe the process of electronic discovery and use e-discovery software to conduct discovery in hypothetical cases.
Use database management systems to organize docketing and scheduling, and document management and retention.
Discuss the need for working in a secure environment, including discussion of ethical considerations, ensuring client confidences, and maintaining computer security.

rows.title: Contract Law
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

describe the manner in which a contract can be formed by “mutual assent”;
differentiate between an offer and a mere expression of interest or an invitation to negotiate;

identify, describe and apply the rules regarding defenses against the enforcement of a contract;

summarize and analyze cases in which a contract can be voided due to grounds such as mistake, duress, unconscionability, statute of frauds and determine whether any such defense is applicable in a particular case;

analyze and apply the rules for contract remedies, i.e., expectation, reliance and restitution damages, to a particular fact pattern and predict the kind of remedy a court will be most likely to order in a particular case;

write proposed code change;
calculate rolling offsets using constants for the angled fittings and 45 degree offsets around
obstruction;

rows.title: American Government and Politics
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Explain the founding and development of the U.S. and California Constitution;
Critique governing institutions and political processes within the United States and California;
Employ introductory political science research methods to contextualize contemporary political issues and operations in the United States and California;
Assess civil liberties and civil rights of individuals and groups as articulated in the U.S. and California Constitutions and subsequent court decisions;
Investigate the role of identity and political ideology in shaping public opinion and public policy in the United States and California;
Analyze how to effectively participate in politics at the national, state, county, and/or city levels;
EXPANDED COURSE OBJECTIVES:
Explain the basic principles of a democratic form of government;
Identify and explain the difference between direct democracy and representative democracy;
Explain the basic principles of the Federal and California Constitutions and place these principles in the context of American history;
Discuss the concept of federalism and evaluate its impact on the American political system;
Describe and assess the process of enacting legislation in the U.S.;
Discuss the concept of separation of powers and identify the roles of the three branches of government;
Describe the unique characteristics of California history, political institutions, party system, and public policy making;
Describe the historical context of United States constitutional amendments;
Identify and explain the concept of civil liberties and civil rights and their application in American society;
Discuss the expansion of suffrage and its impact on government and society;
Describe the development of national political party systems and evaluate the role of political parties in American government;
Describe and assess patterns of voting and political participation in the U.S;
Analyze the roles of the media in contemporary U.S. politics;
Apply course content to contemporary political events locally, nationally, and internationally;
Analyze political issues in a critical and objective manner.

rows.title: Introduction to Political Theory
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: evaluate the study of political theory, based on original texts and other sources, as a means for understanding important political phenomena;
analyze political theory and theoretical texts and explain how they are relevant to contemporary issues;
read, interpret, and evaluate arguments independently and critically;
define their own theoretical commitments in the political realm;
assess the historical and social context surrounding the generation of political theories;
compare and contrast the defining elements of each political theory;

analyze the different assumptions and values about "human nature" and "reality" embedded in each political theory and examine the way these starting premises shape the questions asked and conclusions reached;
evaluate the contribution of political theories toward a comprehensive understanding of political life and institutions.

rows.title: Introduction to Psychology-Counseling in a Multicultural Environment
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: apply Psychology-Counseling theory and techniques;
describe fundamental Psychology-Counseling techniques and theories;
describe methods of effective behavioral change;
identify the demographic composition of one’s campus and environment;
develop a fundamental plan of action with an individual to affect that individual’s behavioral change or desired life change;
assess socio-economic/cultural barriers;
identify local intervention or social service programs;
express the importance of an individualized action plan for behavioral change.

rows.title: Self-Esteem For Success
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Identify origins of self-esteem;
explain two concrete ways or steps that could help someone else improve their self-esteem;
identify self-defeating behaviors that may have a negative impact on their self-esteem.

rows.title: University Transfer Planning
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:

demonstrate understanding of existing transfer opportunities that best meet individual academic and career goals;
demonstrate a knowledge of course-level and program-level articulation issues;
demonstrate knowledge of four-year college and university financial aid, housing, academic and career advising, scholarships, and other programs that support transfer students;

identify proper course sequencing for intended transfer plan;
plan and execute a meaningful site visit to potential four-year institutions;
formulate and present a written transfer plan;
execute, in a timely manner, the appropriate steps of the written transfer plan.

rows.title: Strategies for College Success

rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:

demonstrate ability to use the college catalog and class schedule;
demonstrate understanding of students rights & responsibilities as outlined in the college catalog;
demonstrate knowledge of AA degree, certificate and/or transfer requirements depending on educational goals;
demonstrate knowledge of registration procedures;
demonstrate understanding of how college success is affected by personal values and life variables.

rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:

demonstrate a better understanding of life management skills.

rows.title: Life Transitions

exhibit awareness of academic goals being influenced by internal and external factors such as self concept, friends, family, work, community and available resources;

demonstrate decision making and problem solving skills in the context of transitions;
demonstrate knowledge of how interpersonal relationships are developed and enhanced through an awareness of self and others and the use of effective communication skills;
understand the development of intersecting identities as integrated psychological, social and physiological beings.

rows.title: Social Work and Human Services Fieldwork
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: apply psychosocial theoretical knowledge obtained in the prerequisite and co-requisite course or courses to the fieldwork experience including but not limited to unconditional positive regard, empathy, active listening, and cultural sensitivity;
evaluate the fieldwork experience in relation to pre-requisite and co-requisite course objectives, career plans, and personal growth;
apply ethics, values, and skills that recognize and explore professional use of self;
identify appropriate referral services for a variety of needs;
practice habits of self care and identify signs of burn out or compassion fatigue.

rows.title: Introduction to Psychological Methodology
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

synthesize a body of research findings;
develop and test hypotheses;
demonstrate knowledge of general research designs, experimental and non-experimental methods, and standard research practices;
select appropriate research designs to test hypotheses;

assess the generalizability of study results;
demonstrate proficiency in APA style.

rows.title: Psychology of Personal and Social Adjustment
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: understand and evaluate what self-concept, self-esteem, self-attributions, self-regulations, and self-presentation are and how each affects adjustment and personal development;
describe and compare the major theories about personality and models of psychological adjustment;
analyze and evaluate the dimensions of effective behavior in a complex and culturally diverse world;

describe specific research methods and principles of research ethics for the study of human beings, including the safeguards and the peer-review process in science;
describe and apply concrete examples of psychological perspectives and applications related to personal growth and psychosocial adjustment;
apply psychological principles and develop “new” interpersonal, occupational and social skills for life-long personal growth;
describe the physical and psychological effects of stress;

apply principles of effective communication in interpersonal relationships;
discuss sexual and gender identity spectrum, and expression;
discuss gender similarities, differences, gender roles, and gender stereotypes;
differentiate between individual and sociocultural differences as applied to psychology of adjustment;
distinguish between the most common psychological disorders, impact on individual adjustment and various treatment options.

analyze psychosocial bases of rape, childhood sexual abuse, and prostitution.

rows.title: Religions of Asia
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: explain the history of Hinduism, as well as its scriptures (including the Vedas, Upanishads, and Epics), beliefs (including samsara, karma, moksha, Brahman, and atman), and traditions (including yoga, the caste system, and the pantheon);

explain the history of Buddhism (including the life of Siddhartha Gautama), as well as its scriptures (including the Pali Canon and Sutras of the Buddha), beliefs (including tanha, dukkha, nirvana, the Four Noble Truths, the Middle Way, and anatman), and traditions (including Mahayana, Theravada, Zen, and Tibetan Buddhism);

explain the history of Jainism (including the life of Mahavira), as well as its scripture (the Agamas), beliefs (including ahimsa, karma, asceticism, the three jewels, jiva, ajiva, and religious tolerance), and traditions (including Svetambara and Digambara Jainism);

explain the history of Taoism (including the life of Lao Tzu), as well as its scripture (the Tao Te Ching), beliefs (including yin, yang, naturalism, and wu wei), and traditions (including minimalism and the rejection of formality and hierarchy);

explain the history of Confucianism (including the life of Confucius), as well as its scripture (the Analects of Confucius), beliefs (including Confucian political philosophy and the Confucian virtues of ren, li, yi, xiao, and zhi), and traditions (including the five relationships, family values, and ancestral rites);

explain the history of Shinto, as well as its scriptures (the Kojiki and Nihongi), beliefs (including animism, kami, ancestor worship, and the three sacred treasures), and traditions (including torii, shrines, and State Shinto).

Acquire greater command and fluency of the language and demonstrate communicative skills in Spanish at the intermediate level in reading, writing, listening and speaking;

describe the styles and explain the history of theatrical scenic design;

mix and apply paint using scenic art methods;
create renderings and scale drawings to express their creative ideas;
operate a basic theater audio/visual systems;
express an understanding of the basics of theater lighting, including color and mixing through design renderings, practical
demonstration of instrument use, and verbal explanation;
explain the basics of a theater sound systems;
cooperate effectively as a member of a production and project team;
conceptualize, plan, create and successfully present a portfolio project;
describe the wide variety of career opportunities in technical theater and related fields.

rows.title: Mainstage Production: Acting 3
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:

analyze the play to develop rehearsal techniques within the context of the style of the play;
make acting choices;
set rehearsal goals and evaluate the meeting of those goals;
build collaboration and trust among the ensemble;
encourage fellow players to do their best work;
support the technical rehearsal process.

rows.title: Mainstage Production: Technical Theater Beginning
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate intermediate level of proficiency in the skills required for a technical theater crew;
demonstrate and employ intermediate skills to address the technical demands of a theatrical production;
execute assignment responsibilities in technical rehearsals, during production run, and strike and help others who are less experienced;
demonstrate the ability to work collaboratively in the application of technical elements for a theater production;
demonstrate an ability to take on individual tasks in the construction of one or two elements of theater production with minimal supervision.

rows.title: Introduction to Acting on Camera
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: Understand basic film making vocabulary;
analyze a script for performance on camera;
develop a character for a performance in a scene on camera;
memorize and rehearse a two person scene;
learn blocking in relationship to camera movement;
engage with the camera;
"Slate" on camera;
cold read a script on camera;
hit marks while delivering lines;
perform a basic two person scene with multiple takes.

rows.title: Intermediate Theater for Young Audiences
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: employ leadership among groups creating a theatrical event for children;
perform with accuracy and clarity a theatrical event for children;
express appropriate terminology used in the theater concerning directing, acting, backstage work;
exhibit emotional expressiveness in performance of a play for young audiences;
lead warm ups for rehearsal and performance;
develop multiple characters for performance;
lead talk back discussions with young audiences.

rows.title: Voice for the Actor
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:
outcomes: demonstrate effective breathing in vocalization;
demonstrate clarity in tones;
demonstrate voice projection and volume control as well as pitch and rate control;
demonstrate articulation, variety on vocal ability, and interpretation;
recognize and identify standard American speech sounds;
improvise;
identify period speech.

rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

outcomes: audition for a show;
rehearse individually and in groups; utilize the production needs such as props, costumes, and set pieces;
memorize lines;
work with classical styles of writing, often in verse;
develop vocal strength and clarity needed for classical text;
sustain character details;
create inner life of a character;
demonstrate a strong work ethic and knowledge of the creative process;
evaluate the creative process for himself/herself;
demonstrate collaboration with the director, stage manager and other members of the production staff;
evaluate and analyze a script for rehearsal and performance.

memorize songs;
lead sections in learning music;
ead warmups for ensemble;
rehearse and learn singing parts appropriate for the show being produced;
ehearse and learn dance parts appropriate for the show being produced;
evaluate and analyze a script for rehearsal and performance;
perform for a live audience effectively;
demonstrate leadership through focused work and commitment to project.

Demonstrate the roles of leadership, team play, sportsmanship and other social values related to team competition.
Describe and apply the rules concerning the sport of track and field.
Perform the techniques and execute the strategies necessary to compete in intercollegiate track and field.
Utilize performance enhancing strategies (goalsetting, concentration techniques, etc.) in practice and competition.

Correctly spot teammates in the weight room to prevent injury and overuse while weight training;

Demonstrate eccentric training to strengthen tendons and ligaments to prevent overuse injuries.

develop strategies to work with students from diverse populations;
practice effective verbal and non-verbal communication skills;
facilitate structured tutoring sessions with clearly-defined learning objectives for individuals and groups;
identify and address challenges that arise during a tutoring interaction;
improve tutoring practice through self-evaluation and mentoring.

rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

demonstrate a continued mastery of the course outcomes from TUTR 2A.
develop strategies for thinking through and explaining problems in the subject area;
identify affective barriers to learning: what they are and how they hinder comprehension and retention;
develop verbal and nonverbal strategies to address affective barriers.

rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

outcomes: demonstrate a knowledge of the FITT principles;
demonstrate knowledge of the principles of strength training;
demonstrate proper techniques of the basic form used in muscular endurance training;
track their blood pressure on a consistent basis;
develop and demonstrate a greater work capacity.

rows.title: Advanced Arc, Flux-Core Welding and Blueprint Reading
rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to:

handle welding and shop equipment in a safe manner;
identify common metals, metal alloys and their properties;
demonstrate the proper usage of welding power supply;

produce sound welding performance tests using SMAW and FCAW welds processes in both flat and horizontal positions according to AWS codes;
properly maintain shop and welding equipment.

rows.heading: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to

handle welding and shop equipment in a safe manner;
demonstrate proper usage of welding power supply;
properly identify metals and metal alloys’ weld-ability;

read, understand and apply; blueprints, welding symbols, and shop sketches;

perform welds tests according to procedures used by certified test laboratory.

perform practical performance tests in 1G and 2G using one of the three welding processes mentioned above;
recognize and identify pipe welding discontinuities and defects and employ the proper method of correction;
perform destructive and non-destructive welding test, evaluate and expound the results.

demonstrate an understanding of the principles of stretching and cooling down;
